title: {{NAME}} and the Royal Prehistoric Gardens
moral: The things we preserve for the future are the greatest gifts we give.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a deep burgundy palace coat with gold leaf trim, cream trousers, and polished boots — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The Royal Prehistoric Gardens had been established two hundred years ago when the kingdom's founders discovered that certain deep valleys held temporal echoes: patches of land where prehistoric creatures briefly appeared from time to time, seemingly from nowhere.

Princess Evangeline ran the gardens with the help of a fairy council who had been the official caretakers since the beginning.

She needed a new Royal Recorder: someone to document every prehistoric appearance, its duration, its species, and its condition.

{{NAME}} applied. He was hired because of his handwriting, his animal knowledge, and the fact that he didn't faint when the Triceratops appeared during his interview.

pages.content:
The work was extraordinary and precise.

Every appearance had a protocol: the fairy council detected them first and alerted him, he documented while they managed the perimeter to keep the animals calm.

He learned to distinguish species on sight. He learned which species were calm (most of them) and which were confused (Pterodactyls, in his experience, seemed personally offended by existing in a time that wasn't theirs).

Princess Evangeline reviewed his records each week.

"Your descriptions," she said, on the third week. "They're exceptional. You make them real on the page."

pages.content:
The most significant appearance came in month four: a young Brachiosaurus, clearly unwell, remaining in the gardens for three days instead of the usual hours.

The fairy council used their healing magic, which worked on organic material from any era. Princess Evangeline directed care.

{{NAME}} documented everything, including the methods the fairies used, which had never been properly recorded before.

"You're writing the manual," said the head fairy, reading over his shoulder.

"Somebody should," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
The Brachiosaurus recovered and departed in a shimmer of temporal light.

The fairy council gathered to review the records afterward.

The head fairy said: "In two hundred years of the Royal Prehistoric Gardens, we have never had a complete written record. We have memory and magic. You have given us documentation."

Princess Evangeline said: "This will outlast all of us. Future keepers will know what we knew."

{{NAME}} looked at his notebooks: four months of precise observation.

He thought: this is the best thing I've made.

pages.content:
That evening, walking through the quiet gardens after the fairies had dimmed their lights, {{NAME}} stopped at the spot where the Brachiosaurus had stood.

The grass was slightly compressed still. A few large prints remained.

He crouched and put his hand in one.

Then he stood and walked home, the notebooks under his arm, carrying two hundred years of future knowledge.

In bed, he fell asleep thinking about the Brachiosaurus and the print in the grass, and how the past didn't entirely go away if someone paid enough attention.
